title: Al-Kawthar: abundance
hookLine: We have given you abundance, so pray and sacrifice (Surah 108)
last: AL-KAFIRUN — TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.

lines: A LOSS TURNED INTO AN INSULT.
cards: People can be cruel about grief. In Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had buried his little sons. And some of his enemies, the commentators say, turned that loss into an insult.

They called him abtar: cut off, a tree with no branches, a man whose name would die with him. Imagine hearing that about your children, in the street. The answer came in the shortest surah in the whole Qur'an.
Three lines, ten words in Arabic. And it doesn't start with the insult. It starts with a gift.

teach.b: Surah one hundred eight begins, in Pickthall's translation: Lo! We have given thee Abundance; So pray unto thy Lord, and sacrifice.
Kawthar comes from the root k-th-r, much, many, in an intensive form: not just a lot, but overflowing, more than enough. Commentators give it two meanings, and hold both.

The first is every good thing given to the Prophet: the revelation, his followers, his name. The second is specific. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet dozed off among his companions, then lifted his head smiling.
Asked why, he said a surah had just come to him, and recited this one. Then he asked: do you know what al-Kawthar is?
It's a river my Lord has promised me in Paradise, with abundant good.

teach.h: THE INSULTER IS THE ONE CUT OFF.
teach.b: The third line turns to the insult: Lo! it is thy insulter, and not thou, who is without posterity. The word is the one they used: abtar. Muslim commentators point to what came after.

The Prophet's name is spoken today by well over a billion people, and his family line, through his daughter Fatimah, is honored across the Muslim world, while the men who mocked him are remembered mostly because this surah answered them.
And notice what the gift asks for in return. Not a speech, not revenge.
So pray, and sacrifice: turn toward your Lord, and give something away. When you're told you have nothing, count what you've actually been given.

how: Al-Kawthar is often among the first surahs children memorize and is recited in the prayers; the hadith of the river of al-Kawthar is widely taught.

o: overflowing good, and a river promised in Paradise
an animal sacrifice offered after the prayer
being cut off, with no one to carry your name

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: promised to the Prophet in Paradise

s: al-Kawthar is the shortest surah in the Qur'an
three lines, ten words in Arabic.
the surah begins by answering the insult
it begins with a gift: We have given thee abundance.
the Prophet smiled when this surah came to him
he lifted his head smiling and recited it (Muslim).

games.q: enemies call the Prophet abtar, cut off, after his sons die. what does the surah do first?
o: name what he's been given: abundance
games.why: it opens with a gift, asks for prayer and giving, and only then says the insulter is the one cut off (108:3).

practice: Count your abundance slowly, on your fingers if you like: first the things that are easy to miss, breath, your hands, water from a tap; then people, one who loves you, one who taught you something; then small good things from this week.
When you run out of fingers, keep going. If you pray, you can end with alhamdulillah.

wordCard.voice: Al-Kawthar. Abundance, overflowing good, and a river promised to the Prophet; the name of the shortest surah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: abundance, overflowing good, from k-th-r, much or many.

carryVoice: Your line: given plenty. The gift came before any answer to the insult. One hundred sixty-six days now.
